strengths: Novel mechanistic approach to understanding and defending against typographic attacks, providing genuine interpretability through layer-wise analysis and identification of specialized attention heads
Training-free method scales to billion-parameter models on consumer hardware, eliminating expensive retraining/fine-tuning requirements for deployment
Comprehensive experimental scope across five model sizes (ViT-B to ViT-BigG) with multiple real-world attack datasets (RTA-100, Disentangling, PAINT-DS)
Rigorous mechanistic analysis with linear probes clearly showing abrupt emergence of typographic understanding in second-half layers, supported by intrinsic dimensionality analysis
Strong reproducibility practices including model release, code availability, extensive appendices with per-model analysis, and clear algorithmic description
Well-presented work with effective visualizations (particularly Figures 2-3) that clearly communicate the mechanistic findings
weaknesses: Critical scope limitation: defense only prevents typographic information from reaching CLS token while leaving spatial tokens intact, severely limiting applicability since many VLMs (LLaVA, IP-Adapters) leverage spatial tokens

Method underperforms the only compared baseline (Defense-Prefix) on most typographic benchmarks (Table 4: 65% vs 82.78% on Disentangling; 69.09% vs 71.82% on PAINT), raising questions about practical superiority

Synthetic dataset bias in circuit construction: Typographic Attention Score computed on ImageNet-100-Typo with fixed bottom-center text positions, not validated on variable text positions/styles found in real attacks
Incomplete causality demonstration in Section 6.2.1: attention manipulation (α redistribution) is indirect; direct head ablation experiments would provide stronger evidence
Very small evaluation datasets (RTA-100: 1,000 images; Disentangling: 180; PAINT-DS: 110) with no error bars, confidence intervals, or multiple runs—insufficient for robust statistical claims
Hyperparameter selection lacks justification: ϵ = 0.01 threshold appears arbitrary with no sensitivity analysis; control dataset uses 5% of ImageNet-100 train without justification
No evaluation on actual VLM tasks or jailbreaking scenarios despite being primary motivation; claims about safety-critical applications unvalidated on real downstream tasks
Missing baseline comparisons to other mentioned defenses (fine-tuning [19], weight interpolation [19], Sparse Autoencoders [22]); only Defense-Prefix compared
Unclear generalization: circuits identified on ImageNet-100-Typo; no analysis of transfer to other datasets or cross-model generalization
Greedy circuit construction (Algorithm 1) with no investigation of optimality or sensitivity to head addition order
Technical clarity gaps: how is indicator function 1(t) computed for RTA-100 and PAINT-DS datasets? Not clearly specified
Multiple writing issues including 'behaivor' misspellings and 'dislexic' instead of 'dyslexic'; Appendix figures 8-12 extremely dense and difficult to parse

strengths: Novel mechanistic approach to adversarial robustness using circuit identification and causal intervention rather than black-box methods
Training-free defense method enabling seamless scalability to billion-parameter models without finetuning
Thorough empirical validation across multiple model scales (ViT-B to ViT-BigG) and diverse real-world attack benchmarks (RTA-100, Disentangling, PAINT-DS)
Consistent improvements in typographic robustness (5.5-32.78%) with minimal degradation on non-typographic benchmarks (<1%)
Convincing causal analysis through attention pattern manipulation experiment demonstrating fine-grained control over typographic vulnerability
Interesting mechanistic insights into how CLIP processes typography: sharp emergence in second half of layers, attention layers add information while MLPs compress it
Clear presentation with effective visualizations and practical contribution via released dyslexic CLIP models
weaknesses: Fundamental practical limitation: defense only protects cls token, while modern VLMs (LLaVA, IP-adapters) use spatial tokens allowing typographic information to propagate to downstream tasks, severely limiting real-world applicability

Incomplete baseline comparisons: only Defense-Prefix quantitatively evaluated in detail; other methods [18, 19, 22] lack comparison; Defense-Prefix outperforms on some metrics (Disentangling: 82.78% vs 65.00%)
Limited methodological novelty: Typographic Attention Score adapted from prior work [30], circuit construction is straightforward greedy search, relatively simple conceptually despite being effective

Evaluation concerns: no adaptive attacks tested against an adversary aware of the defense; synthetic datasets (ImageNet-100-Typo with random text placement, Unsplash-Typo with fixed bottom position) may bias head selection toward specific patterns
Arbitrary hyperparameter choices without justification: ε=0.01 threshold selected without sensitivity analysis, 5% dataset subset not motivated, unknown robustness to these choices
Incomplete ablation studies: no sensitivity analysis for threshold ε, limited exploration of circuit sparsity (4.2-10.2%), no comparison of alternative ranking criteria
Limited scope: only OpenCLIP models tested (generalization to ALIGN, LiT, SigLIP unknown); primarily zero-shot classification evaluated (retrieval, generation applications not tested)

Attention sink mechanism underexplored: mechanistically interesting finding (Appendix B) but disconnected from main narrative, mechanism explanation lacking, unclear why this pattern emerges during training
Missing deeper analysis: why CLIP learns typographic circuits unexplored, connection between circuit sparsity and vulnerability not examined, limited discussion of failure modes on certain datasets
Reproducibility concerns: relies on very recent Prisma library [29] from 2025, limited hardware specifications provided, unclear generalization beyond OpenCLIP models

strengths: Novel application of mechanistic interpretability to adversarial defense with solid experimental validation across five model sizes and multiple datasets, achieving up to 31% improvement on real typographic attacks
Insightful mechanistic analysis elegantly revealing how typographic understanding emerges abruptly in model's second half through linear probes and intrinsic dimensionality measurements
Comprehensive causality demonstrations via attention manipulation experiments (Fig. 5) convincingly linking identified heads to typographic vulnerability
Practical gradient-free approach with zero inference overhead, 3.8x speedup over Defense-Prefix, and scalability to billion-parameter models
Honest discussion of limitations and transparent acknowledgment of cls-token-only scope, reduced OCR capabilities, and VLM applicability concerns
weaknesses: OCR+blur baseline (Appendix J) outperforms Dyslexify on ImageNet-100-Typo (68.52% vs 66.84% ViT-B), undermining practical advantage claims and suggesting pixel-level defenses may be preferable
Severe limitation to cls token only significantly restricts applicability to deployed VLMs (LLaVA, IP adapters) that use spatial tokens, as acknowledged by authors, limiting real-world impact

Adaptive attacks not evaluated; unclear whether attackers aware of the mechanism could exploit spatial tokens or target specific heads; claimed non-differentiability of attacks needs stronger justification

Generalization concerns: circuits identified on ImageNet-100-typo show high variance across datasets (3.45%-31.11% improvement); no analysis of transfer to different typographic attack modalities or prediction of which characteristics enable transfer

Limited technical novelty: circuit ablation is established technique; Typographic Attention Score directly adapted from prior work; core method is straightforward head identification and iterative ablation with arbitrary hyperparameters (ε=0.01, k=10) lacking sensitivity analysis
Localization mask requirement for T_i,ℓ computation (Eq. 7) is impractical without external OCR (PaddleOCR), contradicting claims of being OCR-free and introducing unanalyzed robustness dependencies

Incomplete adversarial evaluation: only Defense-Prefix compared in main text; Table 3 shows mixed results (Dyslexify better 2/3 typographic, DP better 2/3 non-typographic); other prior defenses not evaluated

Medical application limited to binary classification and single foundation model; unclear threat model for when typographic attacks occur in practice; different vulnerability levels across datasets (Fig. 10b) suggest fragility
Missing ablations on adversary knowledge of circuit structure, robustness to OCR errors, or whether remaining 90% of attention heads could be exploited; sparse circuits analysis incomplete
Reproducibility gaps: code availability status unclear; circuit construction is dataset-specific; implementation details sparse regarding attention sink detection and mask generation
